facts.one_liner: Whitsunday Island’s ~7 km silica-sand shore—white sand, turquoise shallows, forested hills.
facts.why_go: Whitehaven Beach runs along the south-east side of Whitsunday Island inside Whitsunday Islands National Park, in the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area. The photo matches the classic day-trip scene: brilliant white silica sand, clear turquoise shallows, green forested ridges across the bay, and tour boats and yachts at anchor. Tourism Whitsundays notes the sand is renowned as pure silica that stays cool underfoot, and many full-day trips pair the beach with nearby Tongue Bay and the Hill Inlet lookout for the swirling sand-and-tide view. There is no public ferry; visitors arrive by commercial tour, yacht, or scenic flight from Airlie Beach, Hamilton Island, or Daydream Island.
facts.best_time: April–October for milder temperatures and lower humidity. November–March is warmer and wetter; marine-stinger risk is higher roughly November–May—follow crew and park safety advice.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Whitsunday Coast Airport (Proserpine) for Airlie Beach/Shute Harbour, or Great Barrier Reef Airport on Hamilton Island. From Airlie Beach, Shute Harbour, Hamilton Island, or Daydream Island, join a boat, high-speed, sailing, or scenic-flight day trip—there is no scheduled public ferry direct to Whitehaven.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable national-park beach (day-use and camping by permit). Anchor access is possible at all tides; nearest public moorings are at Tongue Bay. Check Queensland Parks alerts and marine forecasts before departing; wear protective clothing when swimming in stinger season.

facts.why_go: Navagio (Shipwreck Beach) is Zakynthos’s most photographed west-coast cove: a crescent of pale shore cupped by towering limestone cliffs above intense turquoise water. The landmark in the photo is the rusting hull of the Panagiotis, which ran aground here in 1980 and still sits mid-beach. Visit Greece notes the classic approaches by boat from Agios Nikolaos, Porto Vromi, or Zakynthos Town, plus the clifftop observation platform that frames the postcard aerial angle. The cove remains a top highlight for photography even when landing is restricted.
facts.best_time: May–October for boat season and clearer seas; early morning for softer light and fewer vessels. Outside summer, weather and operator schedules vary—confirm before travelling.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly or ferry to Zakynthos (Zante). Reach the free clifftop viewpoint by road on the north-west coast. Boat excursions toward the cove traditionally depart Porto Vromi, Agios Nikolaos, or Zakynthos Town—follow current Port Authority rules on approach distance.
facts.good_to_know: VIEWABLE but NOT landable (2026): Greek authorities have banned visitor access to the beach and swimming in the cove through 31 October 2026 due to rockfall risk; vessels must keep a prescribed distance from the shore. The upper observation platform is the permitted land-side viewpoint once protective fencing is in place—check Visit Greece / local notices before you go.

facts.one_liner: Galicia’s Praia das Catedrais—layered rock arches and caves revealed at low tide.
facts.why_go: Cathedrals Beach (Praia das Catedrales / As Catedrais) near Ribadeo on Galicia’s Cantabrian coast is named for the monumental natural arches and buttress-like cliffs carved from horizontally layered rock. The photo matches that Atlantic drama: dark, stacked sedimentary walls, wet sand at low tide between the formations, and churning green sea under a heavy sky—not a tropical bay. Turismo Ribadeo stresses that the caves, islets, and cathedral-like arches are fully revealed only when the tide drops. It is a Xunta de Galicia natural monument, free to visit with seasonal capacity controls.
facts.best_time: Plan around low tide—ideally arrive about an hour before low water (check the official tide table). Outside July–September and Semana Santa you usually avoid free-reservation crowds; spring and autumn can be dramatic for photos.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Ribadeo (Lugo province). Drive or bus along the coast to the As Catedrais parking/access area west of town; walk down to the sand only when the tide allows. Nearest major airports include Asturias (OVD) or A Coruña (LCG), then road transfer.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable natural monument. Free advance reservation is required during Semana Santa and 1 July–30 September via the Xunta site (ascatedrais.xunta.gal); rest of year access is generally open under local rules. Never get cut off by the rising tide—watch times and lifeguard flags.

facts.good_to_know: Fully public urban beach open year-round. Use normal big-city caution with belongings; swim where conditions and lifeguards allow. The calçadão is a landmark in its own right for walking and people-watching.

facts.why_go: Bondi Beach is Sydney’s best-known eastern-suburb shoreline: a broad crescent of golden sand facing the Tasman Sea, backed by cafés, the pavilion, and apartment blocks climbing Ben Buckler headland. The Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk starts here and threads south past Tamarama, Bronte, and Clovelly.
facts.best_time: Spring and autumn for warm days without peak-summer density; summer (Dec–Feb) is prime swimming and surfing but busiest. Early mornings are quieter; Sculpture by the Sea runs along the Bondi–Tamarama cliffs in October–November.

facts.good_to_know: Fully public, patrolled beach. Swim only between the red-and-yellow flags; Bondi has strong rips, especially near the southern end. Lifeguard hours vary by season—check Waverley Council beach info before entering the water.

Lifeguarded sections and a dense resort strip make it one of Hawaii’s easiest first-beach stops.

facts.why_go: Railay (Rai Leh) is a limestone peninsula on the Krabi coast, cut off from the mainland by cliffs so there are no roads in—only boats. West Railay (West Rai Leh) is the broad, swimmable bay shown in the photo: pale golden sand, calm turquoise water, and sheer karst walls rising over the beach with more jagged limestone across the bay. Sunbathers pack the shore on clear days; rock climbers base nearby at Tonsai and East Railay. Tourism Authority of Thailand lists Railay among Krabi’s signature Andaman attractions, typically reached by longtail from Ao Nang.
facts.best_time: November–April is the drier Andaman season with calmer seas for boat transfers. May–October brings more rain and occasional rough crossings; mornings are usually quieter on West Railay sand.

facts.good_to_know: Publicly visitable; no road access—expect to wade ashore from longtails at some tides. West Railay suits swimming and sunsets; East Railay is muddier and more about climbing access. Confirm last return boats before dusk.

facts.one_liner: Harbour Island’s Atlantic shore—pale pink sand from crushed foraminifera shells.
facts.why_go: Pink Sands Beach runs more than three miles along Harbour Island’s eastern Atlantic coast, typically 50–100 feet wide, and is the island’s signature natural attraction. Official Bahamas tourism explains the pale pink tone as crushed remains of Foraminifera—tiny marine organisms with pink or red shells—washed ashore from nearby reefs such as Devil’s Backbone and mixed with coral sand; the colour shows best in wet sand at the waterline. The photo’s empty diagonal shoreline, soft pink foreground, and turquoise-to-deep-blue gradient match that quiet Atlantic stretch rather than a crowded hotel pool beach.
facts.best_time: December–April is the drier peak season with reliable sunshine; May–November is warmer and wetter, with hurricane-season awareness from roughly June–November. Soft morning or late-day light deepens the pink tone for photos.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly to North Eleuthera (ELH), taxi to Three Island Dock / Government Dock area, then a short water taxi to Harbour Island. From Dunmore Town, walk, taxi, or golf cart east to the beach. Alternative: Bahamas Ferries from Nassau on scheduled sailings—confirm current timetable.
facts.good_to_know: Publicly accessible beach. Sand is often cool underfoot per Bahamas tourism notes. Bring reef-safe sunscreen; Atlantic swells can be stronger than the island’s sheltered west side—swim with care and local advice.

facts.one_liner: Haystack Rock at Cannon Beach: 235-ft basalt stack, Needles, and Oregon tidepools.

At low tide you can walk the wet sand to tidepools teeming with anemones and stars, while tufted puffins and other seabirds nest on the rock in spring and summer. No overnight parking at Tolovana.
facts.good_to_know: PUBLIC / OPEN — Oregon ocean shore is public; climbing above the barnacle line / nesting rock is prohibited. Walk on sand only in tidepools; no collecting. Pets on leash; drones banned near nesting birds at Tolovana/Haystack area.

facts.one_liner: Jurassic Coast Dorset—Portland limestone arch and pebble beach near West Lulworth.
facts.why_go: Durdle Door is the famous natural limestone arch on Dorset’s Jurassic Coast UNESCO World Heritage shoreline near West Lulworth—sea-cut Portland limestone with the beach and arch readable together. The Lulworth Estate describes the cliff path down to Durdle Door beach (and steps to Man O’War), chalk cliffs, and wave-cut caves; do not enter caves—cliff falls are common. The hero is a sunset frame of the arch and shore (Commons: Durdle Door Dorset Sunset)—Dorset Jurassic Coast, not Cornwall.

facts.one_liner: Namibia’s foggy Atlantic wilderness—Namib dunes meeting surf along the Skeleton Coast.
facts.why_go: Skeleton Coast Park runs roughly 500 km from the Ugab River to the Kunene, about 40 km inland—one of Namibia’s great wilderness coasts of fog, cold Benguela Current air, windswept beaches, dunes, and ephemeral riverbeds (MEFT; Visit Namibia). Public lodging hubs at Terrace Bay; northern wilderness is largely fly-in concession country.
facts.best_time: Year-round cool coastal climate with frequent fog. Dry inland winter (roughly May–October) suits self-drive park days; summer heat inland contrasts with cold sea air on the shore.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Swakopmund for the southern Atlantic coast and park approaches via the C34 toward Ugabmund. Skeleton Coast Park entry requires booking/permit arrangements—confirm MEFT/NWR rules. Terrace Bay is the main public rest camp inside the park; north of there is restricted wilderness access.

facts.one_liner: Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē—Northland’s vast Tasman surf beach and dunes (not Victoria, Australia).
facts.why_go: Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē / Ninety Mile Beach is the long west-coast strand of New Zealand’s Far North—about 88 km from near Ahipara north toward Scott Point, despite the “ninety mile” name (dual name under Treaty settlement; DOC; Tourism NZ references). The hero looks south from the hill at Hukatere: expansive surf, sand, and dunes with no vehicles in frame (Commons: Ninety Mile Beach at Hukatere2). It is a taonga co-governed by Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē Board and a Te Araroa walking section—not Ninety Mile Beach in Victoria, Australia.
facts.best_time: Summer (Dec–Feb) for long daylight and beach weather—also the busiest. Shoulder months often mean fewer people and still walkable conditions; always check tides and wind.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly or bus to Kaitaia; Ahipara sits at the southern end (~15–20 minutes west). Access points include Waipapakauri Ramp and Te Paki Stream (north). facts.good_to_know: Treat it as a reserve and privilege, not a highway—check tide times, keep speed low near ramps, and never drive near high tide on soft sand. No camping on the beach or dunes. Patchy mobile coverage. Hukatere viewpoint matches the hero’s elevated dune-and-surf look.

facts.one_liner: Baunei’s tiny Golfo di Orosei cove—turquoise water under the Aguglia limestone pinnacle.
facts.why_go: Cala Goloritzé is the protected pebble-and-sand cove on Sardinia’s Golfo di Orosei coast in the Municipality of Baunei, famous for the soaring Aguglia (Punta Caroddi) limestone pinnacle above turquoise water. Turismo Baunei’s official trail starts at Su Porteddu on the Golgo Plateau; boats may not land on the beach. The hero shows the tiny cove, clear water, and landmark pinnacle (Commons: Cala Goloritzé 1)—this named cala, not Cala Mariolu or other Orosei coves.
facts.best_time: Late spring through early autumn for trail access and swimming; midsummer is hottest and booking pressure is highest. Start early—trail opening hours are limited.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Baunei or Santa Maria Navarrese. Drive to the Golgo Plateau / Su Porteddu trailhead parking, then hike ~3.5–3.6 km one way (~1.5 hours down, ~2 hours up; ~500 m elevation change). Mandatory advance booking via Heart of Sardinia (app/website). Return by boat from the beach is not allowed.
facts.good_to_know: Closed-toe grip shoes and plenty of water are required guidance from Turismo Baunei. Capacity and timed access apply; keep your booking QR. Stay on marked paths; the Aguglia is a climbing landmark—do not scramble unsafely. Distinct from nearby Cala Mariolu.

facts.why_go: Muri Beach fronts Muri Lagoon on Rarotonga’s southeast coast (Ngatangiia), the island’s busiest lagoon strip with calm, shallow water and a string of motu—Motutapu, Oneroa, Koromiri, and Taakoka at the southern edge. facts.how_to_get_there: International flights into Rarotonga (RAR). Muri is on the southeast coast via the coastal ring road (~20–30 minutes from the airport depending on traffic). Scooters and rental cars circle the island easily; many visitors stay in Muri itself.
facts.good_to_know: Lagoon is very shallow in places—great for beginners, limited for deep swimming. Water-quality issues have affected Muri Lagoon in past years; check current local advisories before swimming or harvesting seafood. Respect motu and reef; leave no litter.

facts.one_liner: Grenada’s long south-coast Caribbean strand—two miles of soft white sand near St. George’s.
facts.why_go: Grand Anse Beach is Grenada’s signature south-coast strand—about two miles of white sand and calm turquoise water in the southern tourism belt near St. George’s (Grenada Tourism Authority). Pure Grenada highlights swimming, beach bars, resorts, the craft and spice market, and sunset views under palm, almond, and sea grape. The hero shows the wide Caribbean strand and bay context rather than a hotel-frontage crop (Commons: Grand Anse Beach Grenada).
facts.best_time: Dry season roughly January–May is peak beach weather. June–November is wetter (Atlantic hurricane season)—still swimmable many days, but watch forecasts.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Maurice Bishop International (GND). Grand Anse is a short drive south of St. George’s / the airport corridor; taxis, buses, and rental cars serve the beach strip. Many hotels sit directly on or across from the sand.
facts.good_to_know: Public beach with resort and vendor zones—loungers may be hotel-managed. Keep valuables secure; use reef-safe habits if snorkelling. Carriacou/Petite Martinique recovery notes after Hurricane Beryl are separate from this mainland Grenada strand—confirm inter-island travel if combining islands.

facts.one_liner: Railay Peninsula’s southern cove—karst cliffs, Princess Cave shore, turquoise bay (≠ Railay West).
facts.why_go: Phra Nang Beach (Ao Phra Nang / Phra Nang Cave Beach) sits at the southern tip of Krabi’s Railay Peninsula—white sand between towering limestone cliffs with Tham Phra Nang Nok (Princess Cave) shrine at the eastern end. Tourism Authority of Thailand materials and peninsula guides treat Phra Nang as its own beach, separate from West Railay and East Railay (boat-only peninsula). The hero shows karst cliffs and the cave shoreline (Commons: Phra Nang beach 1)—distinct from the Railay Beach card (beaches-008).
facts.best_time: November–April dry season is clearest and busiest; early morning or late afternoon dodges day-trip boat crowds. May–October brings more rain and fewer people.
facts.how_to_get_there: No road access. Longtail boats from Ao Nang (~15 minutes) or from Krabi Town / Ao Nam Mao piers land at Railay, then walk ~5–10 minutes to Phra Nang (East path under cliffs, or via West/Rayavadee side). Fly into Krabi (KBV).
facts.good_to_know: Not the same beach as Railay West/East—same peninsula, different cove. Princess Cave is a free open shrine; be respectful with offerings and photos. Limited facilities on Phra Nang itself—nearest toilets toward Railay East. Check tide if walking toward the small offshore islets.

facts.one_liner: Lagos Algarve cove—ochre cliffs, turquoise water, and a steep wooden stair to the sand.
facts.why_go: Praia do Camilo is a compact double cove on the cliffs south of Lagos, golden-ochre limestone walls dropping to sheltered Atlantic sand—classic Algarve gold-coast scenery promoted via Visit Portugal / VisitAlgarve listings. Reach the sand by a long wooden staircase from the clifftop car park/viewpoint; a rock arch/tunnel often links the twin coves. The hero shows cove, ochre cliffs, and readable beach (Commons: Strand Praia do Camilo Lagos)—Lagos Camilo, not Praia da Marinha (beaches-024).
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for swimming with lighter crowds. July–August is busiest; parking fills early. Winter brings dramatic seas but cold water.
facts.how_to_get_there: Base in Lagos. Drive or taxi toward Ponta da Piedade / Camilo signs south of town; limited clifftop parking. Walk the wooden steps down to the sand. Faro (FAO) is the main Algarve airport (~1 hour by car).
facts.good_to_know: Steep stairs—not ideal with heavy gear or limited mobility. Stay away from cliff edges and bases (rockfall risk on Algarve arribas). Distinct from Praia da Marinha further east. Seasonal café/facilities at the top; bring water for the climb back up.
